variables_mentioned: age at the beginning of the employment spell

linkages: Employment records from the SPELL register are combined with incarceration records from the KRIN register at the individual level to track employment and imprisonment histories.

Employment records with gaps of less than a week or overlaps of more than a month are treated as part of the same job; on-the-job search is identified by two employment records with a gap or overlap of less than a month.

sample.universe: Male individuals aged 15 to 35 in Danish register data from Statistics Denmark, 1986-2003, with employment records in the SPELL register.
sample.unit_of_observation: Individual (one first observed employment spell per individual for the wage regression; individual spell sequences - incarceration duration t_0, unemployment duration t_1, employment duration t_2 - for the maximum likelihood estimation).
selection_rules: Danish register data covering 1986-2003 (start and end dates of employment and incarceration spells).
Restricted to male individuals aged 15 to 35, 'as crime rates decline significantly after age 35'.
Workers without criminal records are those with no incarceration records between 1986 and 2003; individuals with an incarceration record during the period are ex-offenders.
Individuals are included from the first instance they become unemployed after 1 January 1986.
Only workers with a job worked for at least 7 days according to the SPELL records are included.
The 10th and 90th percentile of the wage residuals are excluded to avoid extreme cases.
Unemployed individuals with no employment records are excluded from the data.
sample.n_observations: 1,726,923 (Table A.1 N and Table A.2 full-sample observations)
sample.n_individuals: 23,522 ex-offenders and 1,703,401 workers without criminal records (Table A.2)

construction_notes: Hourly wage is measured in the first observed employment spell after 1 January 1986, or in the first employment spell beginning after release from prison for ex-offenders; it enters the Mincerian regression in logs.

Wage residuals from the Mincerian regression (which strip out age, education and job type) are the empirical object the structural model is calibrated to; Table A.3 reports max 2.1865, min 0.3595, mean 1.2161 and the residual at the productivity cutoff 1.6121 as calibration targets.

Unemployment duration t_1 is the time from the end date of the first employment record to the start date of the second; employment duration t_2 is tracked from the start of the new job; durations are measured in months.
Age enters the wage regression as a quadratic to capture experience effects.

The apprehension probability is calibrated from the ratio of the average number of criminal offenses (138,334.50) to the average number of inmates (3402) over 1986-2003; the overall crime rate is 138,334.50/5,254,250 = 26.3 offenses per 1000 individuals with an average Danish population of 5,254,250.
Standard deviations of the MLE parameters are bootstrapped with 500 draws (note to Table A.3).

links.pointer_quote: Using Danish register data from 1986 to 2003, I first document that, conditional on observed characteristics, workers with a record of imprisonment earn on average 1.92% higher wages than comparable workers with no criminal record.

claims.statement: Conditional on education, age, full-time status and year, men aged 15-35 with an imprisonment record 1986-2003 earn 1.92% higher hourly wages in their first observed employment spell than comparable men with no criminal record.

outcome.label: log hourly wage in the first observed employment spell, log(w_i)

register_source.value: SPELL register (start and end dates of each employment spell), Danish register data from Statistics Denmark

definition.value: 'For each individual, I construct an hourly wage measure from the first observed employment spell after January 1, 1986, or from the first employment spell that begins after release from prison for ex-offenders.' Entered in logs as the dependent variable of the Mincerian OLS regression.

timing.value: First observed employment spell after 1 January 1986 (for ex-offenders: the first spell after release from prison), within 1986-2003.

units.value: log points (coefficient on a 0/1 imprisonment-record indicator in a log hourly wage regression)

magnitude.interpretation: 'the hourly wages of ex-offenders are 1.92% higher than those of workers without criminal records' (p. 3)

estimand.target_population: Men aged 15-35 in Denmark 1986-2003 with an observed employment spell, comparing those with and without an incarceration record.

population.description: Male individuals aged 15 to 35 in Danish register data 1986-2003, observed in the SPELL employment register, split into ex-offenders (an incarceration record 1986-2003) and workers without criminal records.
population.selection: Restricted to males aged 15-35; individuals enter the data from the first time they become unemployed after 1 January 1986; only workers with a job worked for at least 7 days in the SPELL records are included; the 10th and 90th percentile of the wage residuals are excluded; wages are observed only for individuals with an employment spell.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: a cross-sectional comparison of individuals with and without an incarceration record during 1986-2003, conditional on education, a quadratic in age, full-time status and year fixed effects.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the observed covariates (education, age and age squared, full-time status, year), having an imprisonment record is unrelated to the wage determinants left in the error term, so the coefficient β_c recovers the wage gap of interest.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reports only that the estimate is 'precisely estimated and robust to the inclusion of basic controls'; no balance test, no alternative specification and no sensitivity analysis is shown.

key_assumptions.assumption: Individuals with no incarceration record observed between 1986 and 2003 have no criminal record; crimes and incarcerations before 1 January 1986 are unobservable and are assumed away.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in footnote 1 as an assumption following Engelhardt (2010); no evidence is offered that it holds.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on being employed (a wage is observed only in an employment spell of at least 7 days) and on not lying in the tails of the wage-residual distribution; selection into employment is not modelled.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The sample restrictions are stated in footnote 2; the paper does not discuss selection into employment as a threat to the wage comparison.

implies_edges.from: employment in an observed spell of at least 7 days

threats_discussed: Criminal records before 1 January 1986 are not observed, so individuals imprisoned before the data begin may be classified as having no criminal record (footnote 1, p. 3).

estimation.specification: log(w_i) = β_c I_i^{imprisonment} + β_X X_i + FE_t + ϵ_it (unnumbered equation, p. 3); single reported column.

ambiguities: Table A.1 prints *** on every coefficient but carries no note defining the significance levels, so no p-value or threshold can be transcribed.
The paper's title and abstract speak of the 'impact' of criminal records, but the design is an OLS comparison conditional on four observables; Section 2 calls it a documented 'wage gap'.
Table A.1 also reports coefficients on the controls (Age 0.3335***, Full-time 0.2175***, Education -0.0071***); the paper never interprets them, so they are not extracted as separate claims.

evidence.how: Table A.1 prints the coefficient and the standard error in parentheses only; no confidence interval and no p-value is printed, and the table has no note defining the stars.

No mean or standard deviation of the hourly wage is printed for either group: Table A.1 reports no summary statistics, and Table A.2 ('Duration means') reports no wage row despite its note referring to mean wages.

value.normalisation: Reference group is workers with no incarceration record between 1986 and 2003 (I_i^{imprisonment} = 0); year fixed effects FE_t absorb the year baseline; age enters as a quadratic.

key_assumptions.assumption: Transitions out of unemployment follow a Poisson process, so unemployment durations are exponentially distributed with hazard μ_Uπ(1-Γ(ḡ_u^j)) + λ_U^j.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 6.2 as a restriction on the likelihood of the no-record group.

identification.source_of_variation: Observed employment spell durations and realised transition destinations (job-to-job, to unemployment, to jail) of the two record groups, fitted by maximum likelihood to the model's Poisson structure.

key_assumptions.assumption: Exits from employment (to another job, to unemployment, to jail) follow a Poisson process conditional on the current wage w, so employment durations are exponentially distributed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed in the likelihood of Section 6.2; no test of the exponential form is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Ex-offenders draw offers only from the unprejudiced firms' offer distribution F^{NP}(w) while workers without records draw from the mixture H(w) = φF^{NP}(w) + (1−φ)F^P(w); this mapping of offer distributions to groups enters the on-the-job search hazard.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sections 3 and 6.2 as a modelling assumption about prejudiced firms; it is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Employed workers who remain in the same job until the end of the data period are right-censored observations of the same Poisson process.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The data section notes that some workers remain in the same job until the end of the data period; no censoring test is reported.

threats_discussed: Greater job stability of workers without criminal records (many remain in their jobs throughout the sampling period) is offered as a competing explanation for the reversed job-to-job transition rate (p. 10).

estimator.value: Maximum likelihood estimation of the Poisson transition rates of the search-and-matching model, standard deviations bootstrapped with 500 draws

key_assumptions.assumption: Transitions into incarceration follow a Poisson process whose rate is μ_kπ(1 − Γ(ḡ_k^j)), i.e. the product of the crime-opportunity arrival rate, the apprehension probability and the probability that the crime value exceeds the reservation value.

key_assumptions.assumption: Employed workers do not commit crimes while on duty, whereas unemployed workers can commit crimes whenever a criminal opportunity arises, so the crime-opportunity arrival rate is at least as high in unemployment (μ_U ≥ μ_E).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 3 as 'consistent with empirical evidence from Landersø et al. (2017)'; in the numerical exercise μ_E = μ_U is imposed instead.

threats_discussed: The estimation of the transition rate from (un)employment to imprisonment does not allow separate identification of the crime arrival rate (p. 10).
unresolved_confounders: Whether the higher incarceration rate out of unemployment reflects a higher arrival rate of criminal opportunities or a lower reservation crime value cannot be separated, because the crime arrival rate is not separately identified.

identification.source_of_variation: Equilibrium of the calibrated search-and-matching model: ex-offenders receive offers only from unprejudiced firms, which post higher wages when they are a majority (φ = .69).

key_assumptions.assumption: Prejudiced firms experience disutility from hiring ex-offenders and screen them out, so ex-offenders receive offers only from unprejudiced firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the central modelling assumption in Section 3; it is not tested, and firms' attitudes are never observed in the data.

key_assumptions.assumption: When the share of unprejudiced firms exceeds one half, unprejudiced firms attract a larger labour force and, under profit maximisation, post higher wages than prejudiced firms.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Derived from the first-order conditions of the profit-maximisation problem (Lemma 4 and its proof, p. 12); the calibrated share is φ = .69.

key_assumptions.assumption: The calibrated parameter values (productivities y_h and y_l, share of unprejudiced firms φ, unemployment benefits b_0 and b_1) are the ones that match the moments of the wage residuals, given the MLE transition rates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A.3 lists the calibration targets (max, min and mean wage residual, wage residual at ϕ); no over-identification test is reported.
